newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. to call for ban on aiding Israeli settlements.
newsitem.headline: U.N. to call for ban on aiding Israeli settlements.

text.p: The General Assembly was expected to adopt a resolution on Tuesday requesting U.N. members to halt any support, by companies and individuals, for Israeli settlements in occupied territories and to bar any imports produced in the settlements.

The resolution was a followup to a recent report by Secretary-General Kofi Annan that Israel had not abandoned construction at a site south of Jerusalem called Har Homa in Hebrew and Jabal Abu Ghneim in Arabic.

The Assembly, at an emergency special session in April, demanded an immediate halt to work at the site, where Israel planned to build 6,500 homes on land captured in the 1967 Middle East war. Israel said more than 75 percent of the land was expropriated from Jewish owners.

The resolution, to be adopted at a reconvened meeting of the emergency session, would condemn Israel's failure to comply with the demand to stop construction at Har Homa/Jabal Abu Ghneim and repeat that demand.

U.N. members would be requested to "take the necessary measures ... to halt any support for Israeli settlements and their economic infrastructures" by any companies and individuals in their respective countries.
They also would be requested "not to allow any import of goods produced or manufactured in settlements in the occupied Palestinian territory, including Jerusalem."
Only the Security Council can impose binding sanctions.

The Assembly resolution, sponsored by 15 Arab and Moslem nations, would also condemn Israel's "lack of cooperation" with the intended dispatch by Annan of a U.N. mission to the area. He said in his report that conditions set by Israel made it impossible for him to send a special envoy, obliging him to rely on other sources of information.

Hinting at a future attempt to suspend Israel from the 185-member General Assembly, the draft "stresses that all member states, in order to ensure their rights and benefits resulting from membership, should fulfil in good faith the obligations assumed by them" in accordance with the U.N. Charter.

An earlier verson of this paragraph, softened to avoid losing support, would have stressed that "normal participation by a member state in the workings of the General Assembly cannot be carried out" while it violated international law, the U.N. Charter and U.N. resolutions.

The resolution recommended the holding of a conference by parties to the Fourth Geneva Convention, which bars settlements in occupied territory, to ensure respect for the convention. The secretary-general would be asked for U.N. facilities for such a conference and to submit a report within three months.

Israel says the convention does not legally apply to the West Bank and Gaza Strip since they were occupied by Jordan and Egypt, respectively, before the 1967 war and were not under a legitimate sovereign. But it says it observes the convention's humanitarian psovisions.

The resolution also called for "reinjecting momentum" into the stalled Middle East peace process and for the implementation of agreements reached between Israel and the Palestine Liberation Organisation.
The Assembly, as in April, would again be only temporarily adjourned, with the possibility of another resumption at the request of U.N. members.
